patients.label: 27-year-old Caucasian man with three years of periodic right ear exudate after a water skiing accident, diagnosed with V. cholerae O100 otitis media
attribution_limitations: The case text calls the presentation "acute otitis media" while the abstract calls it "recurrent otitis media" (and "chronic periodic earaches"); symptoms lasted three years. These are course descriptors that are not mutually exclusive, not two values of one measurement, so this is an ambiguity, not a source conflict; the condition is recorded as plain otitis media.

"Three weeks later" for the repeat ear swab follows the sentence on ciprofloxacin ear drops used until the symptoms disappeared; whether the three weeks run from the start of the drops or from symptom resolution is not stated. The time anchor is left null and only the ear-drop course is ordered before the swab.
The authors state the patient had none of the complications of untreated otitis media, but no hearing test or other workup is described; recorded as absent with verification unknown, not refuted.

limitations: The article has no figures and no supplements; no visual, figure-EHR, privacy, measurement-series or supplement review applies.

Table 1 lists published literature cases; only its last row (labelled "The current study") concerns the index patient; it repeats the accident place and gives January 2011, and the discussion also states January.
Discussion paragraphs on virulence genes, OmpU and ToxR are mechanistic commentary and are not recorded as patient facts; hedged causal claims are not asserted.
The reference point of "Three weeks later" for the repeat ear swab is not restated in its sentence, so no anchor is recorded.
No dose or frequency is given for ciprofloxacin ear drops; no hearing test, otoscopy or imaging is described.

events.description: Culture growth and identification as V. cholerae by VITEK-2, MALDI-TOF and ompW PCR

evidence.quote: Twelve hours after initial incubation a prominent bacterial growth was noticed on Chocolate agar, Tryptic soy blood agar, and MacConkey agar plates (Novamed, Israel). The suspected bacterium was identified as V. cholerae by means of VITEK-2 bacterial identifier system (BioMerieux, France) and by using Vitek-MS MALDI-TOF technology (BioMerieux, France). Additionally, five single colonies were picked and streaked on Luria (LB) agar (HiMedia, Mumbai) in five successive days to verify the purity of the isolates; then their identities were verified by a PCR assay in accordance with . The results demonstrated that all the strains were positive for ompW, a gene of an outer membrane protein, specific to V. cholerae.
